author: Lovin Kobusingye
title: Africa Can’t Build a Blue Economy Without the Women Who Bring Its Fish to Market
content:
Before dawn, wherever Africa has a coast or a lake, women wait on the shore for the boats. When the catch lands, our work begins. We smoke, dry, salt or ferment the fish, using skills passed down for generations, and carry it to market. We are more than a quarter of the 

12.3 million people

 who work in Africa’s fisheries, and 

58 percent

 of its fish processors.




In July, African ministers meeting in Luanda promised women, youth and local communities at least 

40 percent representation

 in blue economy advisory bodies and financing programmes. The African Union Commission has been tasked with drafting the roadmap to deliver it. Unless that roadmap names women fish processors and traders, and removes the rules that keep us from credit, the promise will pass us by.







 




Many countries still count fisheries only by what happens in the water, so the millions of women who process and trade the catch barely register. But if you are invisible, you receive invisible budgets, invisible investments and invisible policies.




I am one of these women. I run a fish-processing business in Uganda, where our lakes yield more than half a million tonnes of fish a year, more than any other African country’s inland waters. I also represent a network of women fish processors and traders across 46 African countries, and though we are proud of the work we do, we know we can do even

author: Fabrizio Floris
title: Paying to work: bribery and the earnings of Kenya’s informal workers
content:
For many informal workers in Kenya, earning a living also means paying for the right to do so. A motorbike taxi rider, a hawker or a small trader may be asked for money by a police officer or a county inspector. It is not a tax set by law, nor necessarily a fine for an offence. It is an informal payment that becomes part of the daily conditions of running a business. According to the 

World Bank

, informal workers can lose up to 20 percent of their daily earnings this way.




The figure appears in the 

Kenya Economic Update

 published on 4 November 2026, which 

looks at how weak governance holds back growth and job creation

. The report describes a country that keeps growing but where growth struggles to improve living conditions: GDP expanded by 5.2 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, yet 83.8 percent of workers are in the informal economy, where incomes are unstable and protection is thin.




It is worth being clear about where the 20 percent comes from. In the body of the report, the most detailed estimate concerns motorbike riders: sources cited put bribes at between 5 and 20 percent of daily earnings, or KSh 50 to 100 a day, with occasional larger demands on top. These are estimates, not findings of a systematic survey, and the report itself acknowledges that survey evidence on how corruption affects workers’ livelihoods is still sporadic. They nonethel

author: Abdulbagi Mohammad
title: Formalising the RSF: EU Policies and Sudan’s Search for Funds
content:
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are one of the two armed parties in the current war in Sudan. Despite their historic collaborations with multiple domestic and external actors, everyone is washing their hands of them. In this piece, I will try to make sense of the RSF and conclude by associating its institutionalisation with the convergence of goals between Sudan and the EU in the 2010s.




It depends on where you stand to identify the root causes of the formalisation and institutionalisation of the RSF. In 2003, when the war broke out in Darfur, Sudan’s western region, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) received a 

humiliating shock

. The Sudanese government then mobilised Darfurians, who know the geography of the area and who were mobile enough to cope with the insurgents’ tactics. The rebel groups were mostly from non-Arab ancestries, while the bulk of the counterinsurgent militias were Darfurian Arabs including Mohammad Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’ (the current leader of RSF) and others. The counterinsurgency campaign was successful militarily, but against the backdrop of this ‘‘succes’’ the campaign left damaging results. The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant, 

in March 2009

, for Al-Basheer, then the president of Sudan,  for war crimes and crimes against humanity during the counter insurgency. What is relevant here is the governmental admiration for t

author: Eibhlin Priestley
title: After the Revolution, Before the War: Tracing Khartoum’s Syrian Community
content:
On 18 March 2023, Arwa Ahmed, an architect, and photographer of the Sudanese revolution, and I stood chatting in the shade of the Grand Hotel on Nile Street in Khartoum. We had spent the morning jumping in and out of Arwa’s white Hyundai photographing buildings of historic significance for the Syrian community. The quiet of the afternoon was broken as ten trucks, each holding dozens of men in civilian dress drove past us at speed. It was an unusual sight, one that we commented on at the time. Less than a month later, we would realise these men were fighters from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) bussed into Khartoum to battle the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) unleashing hell on the people of Sudan on 15 April 2023. The country has since suffered what UNHCR has described as the most devastating humanitarian and displacement crisis in the world, largely out of sight of media attention.




Entrance to the Grand Hotel, Nile Street, a popular choice for Syrian weddings in the 1950s and 1960s. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.




Eighteen months into my History PhD, I arrived in Khartoum in March 2023 to meet and interview members of the Syrian community whose grandparents or great-grandparents arrived in Sudan from Greater Syria (today’s Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan) at the turn of the twentieth century. I was warmly welcomed into homes with cooling glasses of

author: Joseph Sampson
title: Who Decides What Africa Reads First?
content:
Every morning, someone decides what Africa reads first.




Usually it is not one person. Often it is not a person at all. It is a recommendation algorithm tuned for engagement, a foreign desk deciding which of fifty-four countries deserves a slot today…or a cousin who forwards a voice note to the family WhatsApp group before breakfast.




The continent has no shortage of journalism. What it lacks is a shared front page. And the question of who assembles one, and how, deserves more attention than it gets.




I was born in Ghana and live in the United States, but my relationship with newspapers started very early. My older cousins still brag that I started reading newspapers when I was only six years old. I vaguely remember the age, but I clearly remember the scene.




In 1986, our 15-inch black-and-white family TV was stolen. Overnight, the house went quiet. For entertainment, for company, for anything to do after school, all I had were the newspapers my uncle brought home from work. He would come in with a stack of papers, and I would spread them across the living room floor, sit in the middle and read the 

Daily Graphic, Ghanaian Times

, the weekend 

Spectator

 and the 

Mirror

 from front to back. I feasted on everything. In the early 1990s, when 

The Ghanaian Chronicle

 arrived, I especially waited for whatever the late Paul Ansah wrote. If he wrote it, I read it.

author: Florence Kyei
title: Who Pays When the Applause Stops? Visibility, Power and Ghana’s Black Challenge
content:
The Black Challenge has won African titles, an African Para Games gold medal and a place at the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup. Yet weeks before leaving for Mexico, where they will face Angola, Colombia and Iraq in Group D, Ghana’s national amputee football team is still appealing for financial support.




This is the paradox at the heart of Ghanaian para-football: a team successful enough to bring international recognition and national pride, but not yet supported by a sporting system strong enough to make that success sustainable.




The appeal came at 

the team’s unveiling in Accra on September 28

, where the president of the National Paralympic Committee Ghana (NPC-Ghana), Samson Deen, called on the government to settle outstanding bonuses and per diems and allocate at least 5% of the Black Stars budget to amputee football.




At the same event, 

NPC-Ghana announced bonuses of GH¢10,000 for each player and GH¢5,000 for each official

 under its “Target the Podium” initiative.




Deen also said the Black Challenge “deserves everything that sports winners win for the nation.”







The issue predates the current World Cup campaign. In May 2024, captain Richard Arthur Opentil 

publicly raised concerns about outstanding bonuses and inadequate support

 while the team competed at the Amputee Africa Cup of Nations in Cairo.

author: Goktug Caliskan
title: A Russian state firm will map more than half of Mali. Who will own the data?
content:
Two contracts signed in Moscow give a Russian state firm the job of mapping Mali’s subsoil and building the system that will hold the data. The accounts published so far do not say who will own it.




On 28 October, at the Russia–Africa summit in Moscow, Mali’s Mines Minister, Amadou Keïta, signed 

two contracts

 with Zarubezhgeologia, the foreign-projects arm of the state-owned geological holding Rosgeologia, also known as Rosgeo. The first commissioned geological maps at a scale of 

1:200,000

 of two areas that together cover more than half of Mali, over 24 months. The second, scheduled for eight months, purchased a national geological information system called “Subsoil Management”.




The mapping includes training for staff of Mali’s National Directorate of Geology and Mines. Reuters, relaying the company’s statement, says the information system is meant to let Mali manage geological data, mineral licensing and regulatory oversight. Other reports describe only spatial storage with tools to visualise and analyse the data.




Bamako’s partnership with Moscow has mostly been read through security, from the arrival of Wagner in 

late 2021

 to the Africa Corps, which has operated under Russia’s Defence Ministry since last year. These contracts reach somewhere else: the records of the Ministry of Mines.

author: Carine Kaneza Nantulya
title: Kenya’s 2027 Election: Time to Address the Warning Signs
content:
On August 16, 2026, hundreds of people armed with machetes, guns, and sticks 

attacked

 a convoy carrying opposition politicians and supporters of the Linda Mwananchi movement in Homa Bay county, western Kenya. The attackers killed at least three people and beat and robbed journalists covering the violence. Witnesses said police officers were present but failed to contain the attacks. The incident was among 

a series of violent attacks targeting civil society events and opposition gatherings

 in the months leading up to Kenya’s August 10, 2027, general elections. At least six people have reportedly been killed and dozens injured in these attacks, raising serious concerns about the safety of political participation as the campaign season gathers pace.







I returned to Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, where my colleagues and I have been speaking with people from different walks of life to understand how they view the political and human rights environment ahead of the 2027 elections for president and the National Assembly. President William Ruto is expected to seek a second term, while opposition parties and candidates have already begun mobilizing supporters at rallies across the country.




One conversation, with a 28-year-old woman, stayed with me.




“I will not vote in next year’s elections.”




Her words were clear and definitive. I asked her why.

author: Adetokunbo Abiola
title: Nigeria’s AI Ambitions vs. The Regulatory Void–Who Protects the Citizens?
content:
Last year, scammers launched a deepfake videos of popular Nigerian social media influencer, 

Martins Vincent Otse

, through a fraudulent Facebook campaign. The cybercriminals superimposed a fabricated AI-generated audio on a genuine video of Otse from early 2024.




Martins Vincent Otse




In the cloned voice, Otse introduced an online chatting scheme where viewers could earn up to $1,000 monthly. By cloning the influencer’s face and reputation, the scammers not only harmed Otse’s reputation as a respected influencer, they also preyed on the poverty of many Nigerians, tricking them into becoming a member of an online platform created to appropriate their personal information and savings.




On 

October 5

, to show that the issue still mattered, the Nigeria Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) warned organisations and staff against sharing sensitive data with public AI tools.




As the federal government shapes  its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy with the aim to leapfrog development, doctors and nurses use clinical Al tools without standardised verification methods and companies run systems without Al oversight structures. Banks move transactions to automated and Al-driven solutions to combat soaring transaction fraud and manage financial risk, while




87.5 percent

author: Huyam Salih and Obai Khalifa
title: Africa cannot build a stronger agrifood economy while the livestock sector loses $4 billion a year
content:
Across Africa, the livestock sector supports more than 350 million people. Livestock is much more than an agricultural commodity. For millions of families, cattle, sheep, goats, poultry, and other animals are sources of food and income. They are also productive assets that support trade, processing, services, employment and rural wealth creation. Despite its centrality to Africa’s wider agrifood economy, the systems that govern and influence the continent’s livestock sector remain among the most undercapitalised parts of African agriculture. Africa loses an estimated USD 4 billion every year due to unrealised livestock potential.




Too often, livestock farmers, particularly pastoralists and small-scale producers, are seen through the lens of subsistence and poverty. Investors see fragmented markets, climate exposure and informal production systems and conclude that the risks are too high. The challenge is therefore not only a shortage of capital, but an investability gap: fragmented supply, weak market information, uncertain offtake, and policy and regulatory uncertainty can make otherwise viable opportunities difficult to assess and finance.




Many countries also continue to face widespread circulation of substandard and falsified veterinary products, varying levels of regulatory capacity, high dependence on imported medicines and the escalating threat of antimicrobial res

author: Paula Slier
title: The War in Sudan and the Challenges of Mediation
content:
Less than two months after Sudan’s war began in April 2023, the then African Union (AU) Commission chair, Moussa Faki Mahamat, called it the ‘prototype’ for ‘African solutions to African problems’.




More than three years later, some of the most consequential diplomacy is taking place through processes that extend well beyond the continent: in Jeddah, Washington and through the Quad of the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt.




Africa has not been absent. On 23 September, the current AU Commission chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, co-chaired with US envoy Massad Boulos the first joint meeting of the Quad and Quintet. The Quintet brings together the AU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the United Nations, European Union and the League of Arab States.




So the question is not where Africa is. It is why African diplomacy has struggled to make more of a difference. Part of the answer lies in the African mediation itself: competing initiatives and disagreements over who should lead and how the war should be handled. But there is another problem that no mediator has yet managed to overcome.

author: Albashir Dahab
title: Delayed Rains and Broken Routes: War and Climate Crisis in North Darfur’s Jebel Issa
content:
All names of individuals interviewed for this article have been changed their safety and privacy. 




The Fatal Rain of Wadi Saleh




In mid-September 2026, when rain finally touched the parched soil of Jebel Issa in North Darfur’s Al-Malha locality, it did not bring life, but rather severe ecological and economic devastation.




Under normal conditions along this fragile Sahelian belt, the rainy season begins in mid-June or early July and extends through late September This predictable precipitation serves as the ultimate lifeline for rainfed millet and sorghum farming, as well as the primary water source for livestock grazing across the northern Darfur plains. This year, however, unprecedented climate variability left the skies dry until 12 September.




When a sudden isolated downpour finally struck the western sectors of Jebel Issa livestock already severely weakened by months of starvation, scorching heat, and gruelling treks between depleted pastures and distant wells suffered immediate thermal and physical shock. Over three consecutive days, from 12 to 14 September, more than 420 head of sheep perished in Wadi Saleh alone, with additional unrecorded livestock deaths reported across neighbouring valleys.

author: Chan Tsz Yung Frederick
title: Laying on Thin Water: The Looming Danger of Sub-Saharan Africa’s Subsea Repair Vessel Deficit
content:
Submarine fibre-optic cables (subsea telecommunications cables) handle up to 

99%

 of our global internet traffic and communications, underlining the operations of numerous businesses and institutions across the world. Their continued proliferation will bring higher network speeds and connect more people and regions to digital communications. Yet, whilst the world is on a roll in laying down more of this critical infrastructure, it is severely underequipped in properly maintaining them. Sub-Saharan Africa is no exception. As the region with the 

fastest-growing population

 and a 

large gap

 to fill in terms of internet connectivity, Sub-Saharan Africa is occupying an increasingly important position in the world’s network of submarine fibre-optic cables.




Sub-Saharan Africa in the growing demand for Subsea telecommunications cables repairs




Once a subsea telecommunications cable is laid, many potential costs are incurred: the future need for repairs due to factors such as human activity, natural disasters, and mechanical failure. Filling this role is the 

registered

 fleet of 63 ships that has subsea telecommunications cable repair capabilities, 

60% of which are not solely dedicated to repairs but are also cable-laying ships.

 For Sub-Saharan Africa, it is serviced by the 

44-year-old 

Léon Thévenin

author: Moussa Traoure
title: The Palace Guard Against the Trenches : What the Mutiny in Niamey Revealed
content:
The mutiny that broke out in 

air base 101 in Niamey

 in the night of 29 August 2026 failed. The real question now is to understand why it took place. Those who took up arms against General Abdourahamane Tiani were young soldiers from the front lines, those who fought the ‘jihadists.’ For all of the Sahel, it’s a much more worrying sign than any plot from the army high command.




Until Saturday morning, fighting took place in the Nigerien capital near to Diori Hamani airport, the presidential palace, and the public television channel RTN. 

Loyalists retook control only with the support of the Russian Africa Corps

. 

The state television broadcast

 the live arrest of several tens of soldiers being arrested, most of them extremely young.




Three juntas, one promise




In Mali, in Burkina Faso, and in Niger, soldiers took power putting forward the same argument: civilian leaders had failed in front of the ‘jihadists,’ and the army would now do better. Assimi Goïta carried out two coups in Mali in 2020 and 2021. Ibrahim Traoré took control of Burkina Faso in September 2022 and overturned another putschist, Paul-Henri Damiba. Tiani deposed President Mohamed Bazoum in July 2023.




The French were asked to leave, and the Russians invited to come in. The three countries concerned founded the Alliance of Sahel States and 

withdrew from ECOWAS in January 2025

author: Amadou Diarra
title: Wood for War: How Wagner Was Paid in Central African Forest
content:
On 9 February 2021, as government troops and Russian mercenaries pushed rebels back from Bangui, the Central African Republic (CAR) signed Decree No. 21.044. It gave a young company called Bois Rouge a forestry permit covering 186,596 hectares in the south-western Lobaye region – 

roughly 1,866 km² of tropical forest, an area larger than Greater London

.




Bois Rouge had never logged a tree. What it had, according to the 

US Treasury

, was a patron: the concession was granted in exchange for services the Wagner Group provided to the CAR, at about the same time Wagner fighters and government forces were recapturing territory from the rebels.




Pieced together from sanctions files, customs data and transparency reports, the story shows how Wagner turned battlefield gains into commodities – and why timber proved a poor currency for a sanctioned militia.




A Russian Company with a Central African Face




Flag of the Central African Republic




Bois Rouge SARLU was 

registered in Bangui in March 2019

. On paper it was a local firm with a Central African boss. 

By October 2019

, at a forestry forum in Shanghai, Bois Rouge was listed under ‘Russia’, represented by Russians Artem Tolmachov and ‘Mike’ Vdovin.




A 

UK parliamentary inquiry into the Wagner network

 later named Tolmachov as Bois Rouge’s commercial director. The research group All Eyes on Wagner

author: Suliman Baldo
title: Why Sanctions Are Not Stifling Sudan’s War Economy and What We Can Do About It
content:
Since the outbreak of the brutal civil war in Sudan in April 2023, the US, British, and Canadian governments, along with the European Union and United Nations, have imposed targeted sanctions on some 32 individuals and 20 companies tied to the bloodshed to restrict their access to assets, international finance, and travel. Three and a half years into the fighting, more than two-thirds of Sudan’s population requires humanitarian aid and almost 14 million people have been forcibly displaced, and the need for effective policy responses has never been more urgent.




These sanctions have had some impact. For example, China, citing international sanctions, refused to authorise the sale of its air defence systems by Pakistan to Sudan in August 2025. Turkey refused a deal to sell drones to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) because the group was unable to provide an end-user licence. Succumbing to pressure, the UAE has 

distanced itself

 from some shell companies previously operating as covers for the RSF from its soil.




More often, however, it has been easy for sanctioned entities to obfuscate and manoeuvre around sanctions, sometimes in the very capitals that have issued them.




Earlier this year, a business forum convened in London to mobilise capital to rebuild Sudan’s economy showed how those profiting from the conflict continue to evade sanctions. One of the event’s sponsors

author: Fundi Skweyiya-Gushu
title: Africa’s Cybersecurity Gap Is Not a Treaty Problem. It Is a Readiness Problem
content:
Africa’s digital economy is expanding faster than its ability to protect it. 

INTERPOL’s African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026

, drawing on information from 36 countries, found that artificial intelligence was involved in 55 per cent of reported cybercrimes across the continent. Reported losses rose from $192 million in 2024 to $484 million, while 72 per cent of surveyed countries reported scam centres operating within their borders.




The figures expose a growing vulnerability. Africa’s digital transformation is creating economic opportunities but also expanding the terrain on which criminals operate. The question is whether African institutions can respond collectively when attacks cross borders, exploit financial systems and use AI to target victims at scale.




Morocco Cybersecurity Week

, held in Rabat from 12 to 14 October 2026, placed regional cooperation firmly on the agenda. The emphasis was appropriate. Yet Africa’s challenge extends beyond convening officials and announcing strategies. It is making institutions cooperate effectively under pressure.




Africa does not lack legal frameworks. 

The African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection

, known as the 

Malabo Convention,

 entered into force in June 2023 after years of delays. Morocco, meanwhile acceded to the 

Council of Europe’s Budapest Convention on Cybercrime

author: Sergey Eledinov
title: Sudan: Nobody Hands Over a Gun for Nothing
content:
On 6 October, Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan 

said again

 that there would be no negotiations with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, 

or ‘any other party’

, and that the war would go on until victory. A day earlier, Donald Trump’s envoy Massad Boulos 

had disclosed a meeting with him in Egypt

. Washington is pushing a 90-day humanitarian truce and, according to 

sources cited by Reuters

, made Burhan’s visa for the UN General Assembly conditional on it.




In 1996, General Alexander Lebed 

told the journalist Yevgeny Kiselyov

 on Russia’s NTV that ‘all wars, even hundred-year wars, end in negotiations and peace all the same’. He then asked whether it was worth piling up mountains of corpses only to sit down and negotiate anyway. In August that year, at Khasavyurt, he signed 

a truce

 himself; the 

peace treaty

 followed in May 1997. The troops left, the other side kept its weapons, and the question of Chechnya’s status was put off until the end of 2001. Three years later the war was back.




Khasavyurt is remembered as a breather that the enemy exploited. But a breather works for everyone. The second war was triggered by the 

raid into Dagestan

author: Mohamed Sheikh Nor
title: Somali Man Speaks Out on Mogadishu Streets About El Niño Threats.
content:
Osman Yusuf Oskar‚ wearing a T-shirt with the letters “SUPER EL NINO‚” walks the streets of Mogadishu carrying a megaphone and signs to alert other Somalis of the risks of heavy rains during the upcoming rainy season․




His voice can be heard above the sounds of traffic and crowds, urging others to heed warnings that El Niño-related floods will threaten millions of people in Somalia, primarily children, according to 

Save the Children warns of El Niño floods in Somalia

).




Osman Yusuf Oskar warning a citizen in Mogadishu




Oskar is not a government employee or a meteorologist․ His campaign effort is a solo project to educate others about El Niño‚ a weather phenomenon with which most Somalis are unfamiliar․




“I am not an official or officer at the disaster management center․ I am stepping into their role of volunteering to spread the word to my people‚ who don’t know much about the Super El Niño‚” Oskar said․




Street by street‚ Oskar shares his warning in public settings․ Some people respond to his efforts; others ignore him and go about their business․ Oskar’s signs and megaphone are tools to help laypeople understand technical weather information․




His campaign follows Somalia’s recovery from one of the worst droughts in recent decades․

author: Francis Annagu
title: Nigeria has not decided how to regulate Chinese businesses. Who will decide?
content:
In mid-September 2026, traders in the auto spare parts section of the Lagos International Trade Fair Complex 

protested against Chinese traders who sell directly to customers

. One protester 

said

 the Chinese had ‘built warehouses, rented shops and are now selling as we do as retailers.’ Police called the protesters 

‘a few miscreants’

.




Nigeria already has rules for foreign businesses. But the government has not said what it wants from Chinese businesses, or who will carry out the policy. In the two weeks after the protest, the police, a market board, a minister’s aide and a governor all spoke. None said whether the rules will change. Mining shows the same gap. In both, a policy question is being handled as a policing problem.




Competition over one supply chain

told Premium Times

 that goods from China take two to three months to arrive and leave him little profit. Meanwhile,

N11.01 trillion

author: Goktug Caliskan
title: Why China won’t build its own Wagner in Africa
content:
Attacks on Chinese workers in Mali are testing Beijing’s reliance on African security forces. Russia’s experience there gives China little reason to take on the fighting itself.




On 9 May, fighters from Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), al-Qaeda’s affiliate in the Sahel, stopped buses and trucks at Zambougou, in the Ségou region of Mali about 60 kilometres from Bamako, ordered the passengers out and burned at least 40 civilian vehicles. One passenger 

told Human Rights Watch

 that the fighters sent the travellers on towards the capital on foot, saying they had declared an embargo on Bamako. HRW found no Malian troops in the area.




On 12 May, the Chinese embassy in Bamako 

published a warning

 urging Chinese nationals to leave several mining districts, citing armed attacks and the government’s campaign against unlicensed mining. The incidents occurred in different parts of Mali, but both exposed the limits of state protection beyond Bamako. A 

second notice in July

 reported attacks on foreigners around Kenieba, Bougouni and Foulou. An embassy can tell its citizens to leave. It has far less to offer those who stay.




A 

BBC Monitoring review

 counted 38 Chinese citizens among the 89 foreigners abducted in high-profile cases across Africa in 2025, many of them working in the gold industry of south-western Mali. The figures cover foreign nationals and of

author: Joseph Abraham
title: Eritrea’s Coming Crisis? How the Lifting of US Sanctions Might Spell Trouble for Africa’s Most Opaque State
content:
On 19 September 2026, the United States lifted its sanctions on Eritrea, one of Africa’s most enigmatic and repressive states. These sanctions were imposed by the Biden administration in 2021 for Eritrea’s role in Ethiopia’s devastating Tigray War (2020-22). Opinions vary as to the possible meanings of their removal: is it morally permissible on the part of the US? Will Eritrea’s inhabitants be uplifted by their departure? Is this a portent of a new US-defined political order in the Horn of Africa? Though these are important questions, the greatest impact – and a paradoxically destabilising one – may instead be felt around Eritrea’s octogenarian autocrat, Isaias Afwerki, as predatory officials search for new political openings. The lifting of these sanctions may yet help to push Eritrea into an era of uncertainty.




Eritrean navy




The departure of the sanctions is both controversial and long-awaited. Human rights groups have 

decried

 the decision, citing now-notorious accounts of forced labour, torture and media suppression that have made the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), Eritrea’s ruling party, a byword for authoritarian governance in Africa. The development was, nevertheless, expected. It comes four months after 

Reuters

 

reported

 on an internal US government document outlining plans to lift the sanctions. Eritrea, which 

denounced

 the sanc
